title: Filtering rows
objectives: Filter rows with `WHERE` and combine conditions.
Bracket mixed `AND` and `OR`, and match text with `LIKE`.

screens.prose: A screen for a portfolio only wants shares that closed above £4. Before any SQL, run the filter by eye.
screens.question: Tap the close of every row where the close is above £4.

hints.text: Go down the close column and ask one question of each row: is it above 4?
Only BP and SHEL trade above £4. BARC and VOD are below it.
Tap the three BP closes and the three SHEL closes: six rows.

feedback.correct: Six rows pass: every BP and every SHEL row.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check each close against 4, one row at a time.

byKey.r0c2: 2.15 is below 4, so BARC on 2 March fails the test.
byKey.r4c2: 2.19 is below 4, so this BARC row fails the test.
byKey.r8c2: 2.12 is below 4, so this BARC row fails the test.
byKey.r3c2: 0.72 is below 4, so VOD fails the test.
byKey.r7c2: 0.71 is below 4, so VOD fails the test.
byKey.r11c2: 0.73 is below 4, so VOD fails the test.

explain.text: You asked the same yes-or-no question of every row and kept the yeses. That is a filter. The columns stay as they were; only rows drop out.

screens.title: WHERE
screens.prose:
In SQL your filter is a `WHERE` clause: `SELECT *` `FROM prices` `WHERE close > 4;` keeps the six rows you tapped. Now a liquidity screen:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM prices
WHERE volume > 500000;
```
screens.question: Tap the volume of every row this query keeps.

hints.text: Compare each volume with 500000. Both have six digits, so compare the first digit.
Every VOD row passes. One BARC row does too.
638000, 704000, 527000 and 581000 are above 500000. Tap those four.

feedback.correct: Four rows: three VOD days and BARC on 4 March.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep a row only when its volume is above 500000.

byKey.r0c3: 412000 is below 500000, so BARC on 2 March is dropped.
byKey.r4c3: 389000 is below 500000, so this BARC row is dropped.
byKey.r5c3: 241000 is below 500000. It has six digits, but its first digit is 2.

explain.text: `WHERE` tests each row and keeps those where the condition is true. Four volumes beat 500000, so four rows come back with all four columns.

screens.title: Text needs quotes
screens.prose: Numbers go into a condition as they are. Text is different. You want the VOD rows.
screens.question: Which `WHERE` clause returns the three VOD rows?

options.why: Without quotes SQL reads `VOD` as a column name. There is no such column, so the query fails.
Quotes turn `ticker` into the word 'ticker'. It never equals 'VOD', so no row comes back.

hints.text: Which side is a column, and which side is a value?
Values that are text go in single quotes. Column names do not.
The column `ticker`, bare, equals the text `'VOD'`, quoted.

feedback.correct: A bare column name, a quoted text value.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Quote the text value, not the column name.

byKey.bare: Without quotes SQL reads `VOD` as a column name. There is no such column, so the query fails.

explain.text: Single quotes mark a text value. A bare word is a column name. `ticker = 'VOD'` compares each row's ticker with the text VOD.

screens.title: Two conditions
screens.prose:
Two tests can be joined. `AND` keeps a row only when both are true.

```sql
SELECT *
FROM prices
WHERE ticker = 'BARC'
  AND volume > 400000;
```
screens.question: Tap the date of every row this query keeps.

hints.text: First find the BARC rows. Then test each one's volume.
There are three BARC rows. Check their volumes against 400000.
412000 and 527000 pass; 389000 does not. Tap 2026-03-02 and 2026-03-04 on the BARC rows.

feedback.correct: Two BARC days traded more than 400000 shares.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A row survives only if it is BARC and its volume is above 400000.

byKey.used-or: You kept rows that pass either test. That is `OR`. `AND` needs both, so the VOD rows drop out.
byKey.all-barc: You checked the ticker but not the volume. BARC on 3 March traded 389000, below 400000.
byKey.r4c0: BARC on 3 March traded 389000, below 400000. `AND` needs both parts true.

explain.text: Each BARC row met the second test too: 412000 and 527000 pass, 389000 fails. `AND` keeps the rows that pass both tests, so two remain.

screens.prose:
Your manager asks for "the BARC and BP rows". A first attempt:

```sql
SELECT *
FROM prices
WHERE ticker = 'BARC' AND ticker = 'BP';
```
screens.question: How many rows does it return?

options.why: You read `AND` as the English 'and': BARC rows plus BP rows. SQL tests each row, and no ticker is both.
You kept one ticker's rows. `AND` needs both tests true in the same row, and no row passes both.
The query is valid SQL. It runs and simply finds no row that passes.

hints.text: `WHERE` tests one row at a time. Can one row's ticker be two things?
Take the first row. Its ticker is BARC. Is it also BP?
No row passes both tests, so nothing comes back. The request needs `OR`.

feedback.correct: No row is both, so nothing survives. This request needs `OR`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test one row at a time: can a ticker equal 'BARC' and 'BP' at once?

byKey.six: You read `AND` as the English 'and': BARC rows plus BP rows. SQL tests each row, and no ticker is both.

explain.text: English 'the BARC and BP rows' means two groups added together. SQL's `AND` asks both questions of one row, and no row is both. Write `WHERE ticker = 'BARC'` `OR ticker = 'BP'` to get the six rows.

canvas.caption: What was meant: ticker = 'BARC' OR ticker = 'BP'

screens.title: AND before OR
screens.prose:
Mixing `AND` and `OR` needs care. SQL does every `AND` before any `OR`, as multiplication comes before addition.

```sql
SELECT *
FROM prices
WHERE ticker = 'BARC'
  OR ticker = 'BP'
  AND close > 4.65;
```
screens.question: Tap the date of every row this query keeps.

hints.text: Bracket the `AND` first: `ticker = 'BARC'` `OR (ticker = 'BP'` `AND close > 4.65)`.
Any BARC row passes, whatever its close. A BP row passes only above 4.65.
Three BARC rows, plus BP on 2 March (4.68) and 4 March (4.66). BP on 3 March (4.61) fails.

feedback.correct: Five rows: every BARC row, and the two BP days above 4.65.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Group the `AND` first, then apply the `OR`.

byKey.left-to-right: You read it left to right: (BARC or BP), then close above 4.65. SQL does `AND` first, so every BARC row survives whatever its close.
byKey.all-six: You dropped the close test. It still applies to the BP rows: BP on 3 March closed at 4.61.
byKey.r5c0: BP on 3 March closed at 4.61, below 4.65. A BP row needs both of its tests.

explain.text: SQL read it as `ticker = 'BARC'` `OR (ticker = 'BP'` `AND close > 4.65)`. Every BARC row passes the first part, and two BP rows pass the second. Write your own brackets whenever you mix `AND` and `OR`.

screens.title: Matching text
screens.prose:
`LIKE` matches text against a pattern. In a pattern, `%` stands for any run of characters, even none, and `_` for exactly one.

```sql
SELECT *
FROM prices
WHERE ticker LIKE 'B%';
```
screens.question: Which tickers come back?

options.text: None: no ticker is the text `B%`
options.why: You read `%` as a character. With `LIKE`, it is a wildcard for any run of characters.
You expected `%` to need several characters. It matches any run, including the single P in BP.

options.text: BARC, BP and every ticker containing a B
options.why: That would be `'%B%'`. With no `%` in front, the B must come first.

hints.text: The pattern is a B followed by anything at all.
Which tickers start with B?
BARC is B then ARC. BP is B then P. Both match.

feedback.correct: Every ticker that starts with B.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. `'B%'` means a B, then any run of characters.

byKey.literal: You read `%` as a character. With `LIKE`, it is a wildcard for any run of characters.

explain.text: `'B%'` means: starts with B, then anything. BARC and BP fit, so their six rows come back. In SQLite, `LIKE` also ignores case for plain letters, so `'b%'` matches them too.

screens.title: Write the brackets
screens.prose: Now the right way round. You want the BARC or BP days on which more than 400000 shares traded. The tests also add a busy BP day.
screens.question: Make `query()` return the date, ticker and volume of every BARC or BP row with volume above 400000.

widget.how: Check runs 3 hidden tests on `db`. They compare the rows your query returns and the column names. Then they add a row to the table and run it again. Rows must match exactly, in order.

hints.text: You need an `OR` between the tickers and an `AND` for the volume.
Without brackets, the `AND` binds to BP alone, and every BARC row slips through.
`WHERE (ticker = 'BARC'` `OR ticker = 'BP')` `AND volume > 400000`, after `SELECT date, ticker, volume` `FROM prices`.

feedback.correct: Brackets first, then the volume test applies to both tickers.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Open the first failing test below the editor.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 expects two rows: BARC on 2 and 4 March. If BARC on 3 March appears, the brackets are missing.
byKey.test-2: Test 2 checks the columns: `date`, `ticker`, `volume`, in that order.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 adds BP on 5 March with 451000 shares. It should appear; check the BP half of your condition.

explain.text: The brackets make SQL test the ticker first, then apply the volume test to whichever ticker passed. BARC on 3 March (389000) now drops out. The new BP day passes both.

screens.prose:
You kept rows by testing each one. The pattern is:

```sql
SELECT columns
FROM table_name
WHERE condition;
```

Compare with `=`, `<>`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` or `LIKE`. Join tests with `AND` and `OR`, and bracket any mix.
screens.question: Which clause keeps the VOD rows with a close of at least £0.72?

options.why: `>` drops 2 March, when VOD closed at exactly 0.72. 'At least' includes it.
`OR` keeps rows passing either test, so every BARC, BP and SHEL row joins in.

feedback.correct: Both tests, and the boundary included.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. You need both tests true, and 'at least' includes 0.72.

explain.text: 'At least' is `>=`, so 0.72 on 2 March counts. `AND` makes both tests apply to the same row. Two rows come back: 2 and 4 March.

screens.title: Splitting a rebalance
screens.prose: An index rebalance is split alphabetically between two analysts. Yours are the tickers starting with B. List each one once. The tests add BATS, SBRY and another BP day.
screens.question: Make `query()` return each ticker that starts with B, once, in a column named `ticker`.

widget.how: Check runs 5 hidden tests on `db`. They compare the tickers and the column name, then add BATS, SBRY and BP rows. Rows are sorted first, so any order passes.

hints.text: Two ideas from this level: a pattern for the first letter, and each value once.
`LIKE 'B%'` tests the first letter. `DISTINCT` drops the repeats.
Return the string `SELECT DISTINCT ticker` `FROM prices` `WHERE ticker LIKE 'B%'`.

feedback.correct: Each B ticker once, including new ones.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Open the first failing test below the editor.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 wants BARC and BP, once each. Check for `DISTINCT` and the pattern `'B%'`.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 adds BATS. Listing tickers by hand misses it; let the pattern find them.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 adds SBRY, which contains a B but does not start with one. `'%B%'` lets it in; `'B%'` does not.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 adds another BP day. BP must still appear once.

explain.text: `LIKE 'B%'` keeps tickers whose first letter is B, wherever they sit in the table. `DISTINCT` turns six BARC and BP rows into two tickers. SBRY fails because its B is not first.

ideas: `WHERE` asks a yes-or-no question of every row and keeps the rows where the answer is yes.
`AND` needs both tests true in the same row; `OR` needs either. SQL does `AND` first, so bracket any mix.
Text values go in single quotes. `LIKE` matches patterns: `%` is any run of characters, `_` exactly one.

formula.name: Filtering rows
formula.tex: \begin{array}{l}\texttt{SELECT cols FROM t}\\ \texttt{WHERE (a OR b) AND c;}\end{array}

summary.trap: "The BARC and BP rows" is `ticker = 'BARC'` `OR ticker = 'BP'`. With `AND`, no row can pass.

quiz.prose:
The closes in `prices` are 2.15, 4.68, 26.84, 0.72, 2.19, 4.61, 26.51, 0.71, 2.12, 4.66, 26.90 and 0.73.

```sql
SELECT *
FROM prices
WHERE close >= 4.66;
```
quiz.question: How many rows does it return?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count closes of 4.66 or more.

byKey.strict: You left out 4.66 itself. `>=` includes the boundary.
byKey.bp-only: The three SHEL closes are far above 4.66, so they pass too.

explain.text: `>=` keeps the boundary. 4.68 and 4.66 pass, and so do 26.84, 26.51 and 26.90. That is 5 rows.

quiz.prose:
```sql
SELECT *
FROM prices
WHERE ticker LIKE 'B';
```
quiz.question: The table holds BARC, BP, SHEL and VOD rows. What comes back?

options.why: You read `LIKE 'B'` as 'starts with B'. Without `%`, the pattern must match the whole ticker.

options.text: An error: a pattern needs a wildcard
options.why: A pattern with no wildcard is allowed. It then behaves like `=`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Without a wildcard, `LIKE` matches the whole text.

explain.text: With no `%` or `_`, the pattern `'B'` matches only the text B. No ticker is that short, so no row comes back. `'B%'` is the pattern for 'starts with B'.

quiz.prose:
`prices` has four tickers on each of 2, 3 and 4 March 2026.

```sql
SELECT *
FROM prices
WHERE date = '2026-03-02'
  OR date = '2026-03-04';
```
quiz.question: How many rows does it return?

widget.label: Rows returned
widget.accept: 8: four tickers on each of two days.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A row passes if its date is either of the two.

byKey.and: 0 would be `AND`: no row has two dates. `OR` keeps a row that passes either test.
byKey.one-day: 4 is one day's rows. `OR` keeps both days.
byKey.all: 3 March fails both tests, so its four rows drop out.

explain.text: `OR` keeps a row when either test passes. 2 March gives four rows and 4 March four more. 3 March fails both.

quiz.prose:
A table of UK tickers holds BARC, BATS, HSBA, LAND and VOD.

```sql
SELECT ticker
FROM tickers
WHERE ticker LIKE '_A%';
```
quiz.question: Which tickers come back?

options.why: You treated `'_A%'` as 'contains an A'. `_` is exactly one character, so the A must be second.

options.text: None: no ticker contains an underscore
options.why: In `LIKE`, `_` is a wildcard for any single character.

feedback.correct: A must be the second letter.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. `_` is one character, then A, then anything.

explain.text: `_` takes the first letter, whatever it is. Then the second must be A, and `%` accepts the rest. BARC, BATS and LAND fit; HSBA has its A fourth.
